title: Hedging a position
objectives: Hedge exposure with a correlated instrument.

screens.title: A long you keep
screens.prose: You are long contract A and cannot sell it today. Contract B is liquid. Each dot is one day: B's move across, A's move up. They tend to move together.
screens.question: Which trade in B lowers the risk of your long A?

options.why: You added to the risk. A and B rise together, so a long B doubles the bet.

options.text: Nothing: B is a different contract
options.why: You ignored the pattern. When A falls, B usually falls too, so a short B gains.

options.text: Sell B and also sell A short elsewhere
options.why: You were told A cannot be sold today. B is the tool you have.

hints.text: Does B tend to rise or fall on the days A falls?
The dots run from bottom left to top right.
A short in B gains on the days A loses.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what B does on A's bad days.

byKey.buy: You added to the risk. A and B rise together, so a long B doubles the bet.
byKey.none: You ignored the pattern. When A falls, B usually falls too, so a short B gains.

explain.text: A and B move together, with correlation 0.8. A short in B gains on most of A's bad days. That offset is a **hedge**.

screens.title: How much B?
screens.prose: Sell $h$ pounds of B for each pound of A. What is left is A's move less $h$ times B's: the gaps from the line. Slide $h$ and watch the sum of squared gaps.
screens.question: Which hedge leaves the smallest gaps?

options.why: You used the correlation alone. B moves less than A, so you need more of it.
You used the volatilities alone. The correlation is under 1, so less B is enough.
You over-hedged. At 2 the gaps are as large as with no hedge, the other way round.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide until the sum of squares stops falling.

byKey.rho: You used the correlation alone. B moves less than A, so you need more of it.
byKey.two: You over-hedged. At 2 the gaps are as large as with no hedge, the other way round.

explain.text: The gaps are smallest near $h = 1.0$. That is the correlation 0.8 times A's sd over B's, $2/1.6$. Both numbers matter, not either alone.

screens.title: The hedge ratio
screens.prose:
The slope you found is the **minimum-variance hedge ratio**:
$$h = \rho \, \frac{\sigma_A}{\sigma_B}.$$
With moves in per cent, $h$ is pounds of B for each pound of A. A new pair: $\rho = 0.9$, A moves 3% a day and B 2%.
screens.question: What is the hedge ratio for the new pair?

hints.text: Multiply the correlation by A's sd over B's.
$\sigma_A/\sigma_B = 3/2 = 1.5$.

byKey.rho: You used the correlation alone. Scale it by $3/2$.
byKey.inv: You divided B's sd by A's. A is the one being hedged, so its sd goes on top.

explain.text: $h = 0.9 \times 3/2 = 1.35$: sell £1.35 of B for each £1 of A. B moves less, so you need more than a pound of it. The correlation scales that down, because B only explains part of A.

screens.title: What is left
screens.prose: Back to the first pair, hedged at the minimum-variance $h = 1.0$. That hedge removes the share $\rho^2$ of A's variance, and any other $h$ removes less. The share $1 - \rho^2$ is left.
screens.question: A moves 2% a day. What is the daily sd of the hedged position, in per cent?

hints.text: Find the share of variance left, then take its square root.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The sd scales by $\sqrt{1 - \rho^2}$.

byKey.var: You scaled the sd by $1 - \rho^2$. That share applies to the variance, so take its square root.
byKey.rho: You scaled by $1 - \rho$. The share left is $1 - \rho^2$, and the sd takes its root.
byKey.decimal: 0.012 is 1.2% written as a decimal. The field asks for the number of per cent, so type 1.2 without a % sign.

explain.text: The variance left is $0.36 \times 4 = 1.44$, so the sd is 1.2%. A correlation of 0.8 cuts the risk by 40%, not 80%. Even a strong hedge leaves a real part of the risk.

screens.title: The two-dice game
screens.prose: Six turns on the sum of two dice, size 1 or 2, width 1 to 3, limit 4. Other traders deal within £1 of fair. On the next screen you hedge what you are left holding.
screens.question: Finish the six turns with a P&L of at least £5 and no rule breaks.

screens.title: One for one?
screens.prose: You are long £10,000 of a share that moves 2% a day. The index future moves 4% a day, with correlation 0.8. A colleague says: "Sell £10,000 of the future. Pound for pound."
screens.question: How much of the future do you sell?

options.why: You used a ratio of 1. The future moves twice as much, so £10,000 of it over-hedges: the sd rises to 2.68%.
You used the correlation alone. Scale it by the share's sd over the future's, 2/4.
You put the future's sd on top. The share is what you hedge, so its 2% goes on top.

hints.text: Which moves more each day, the share or the future?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $h = \rho\,\sigma_A/\sigma_B$ with the share as A.

byKey.one: You used a ratio of 1. The future moves twice as much, so £10,000 of it over-hedges: the sd rises to 2.68%.
byKey.inv: You put the future's sd on top. The share is what you hedge, so its 2% goes on top.

explain.text: $h = 0.8 \times 2/4 = 0.4$, and the sd falls from 2% to 1.2%. Pound for pound leaves you short the market: the sd rises to 2.68%, above no hedge at all. Too much hedge is a new position the other way.

screens.title: The hedge rule
screens.prose:
For each pound of A hedged with $h$ pounds of B, the variance left is $\sigma_A^2 + h^2\sigma_B^2 - 2h\rho\,\sigma_A\sigma_B$. It is smallest at
$$h = \rho\,\frac{\sigma_A}{\sigma_B}, \qquad \sigma_{\text{left}} = \sigma_A\sqrt{1 - \rho^2}.$$
Every hedge you cross a spread for also costs edge.
screens.question: Two contracts have correlation 0. What hedge ratio leaves the least risk?

widget.accept: 0: with ρ = 0, h = 0 and no hedge helps.
widget.label: h

hints.text: Put $\rho = 0$ into the ratio.
$h = 0 \times \sigma_A/\sigma_B$.
$h = 0$: B tells you nothing about A.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With $\rho = 0$ the ratio is 0.

byKey.one: You hedged one for one. With no correlation, B only adds its own risk.

explain.text: With $\rho = 0$ the best hedge is none, and $\sigma_{\text{left}} = \sigma_A$. Any B you trade only adds $h^2\sigma_B^2$ to the variance. A hedge needs correlation to work.

widget.solution:
import math
import random


def hedge_ratio(rho, sa, sb):
    """Pounds of B to sell per pound of A (sds in per cent)."""
    return rho * sa / sb


def residual_sd(rho, sa):
    """sd of A left after the best hedge."""
    return sa * math.sqrt(1 - rho ** 2)


def hedged_pnl_sim(rho, sa, sb, h, n, seed):
    """sd of A - h*B over n seeded days.
    rng = random.Random(seed); each day draw
    z1 = rng.gauss(0, 1), then z2 = rng.gauss(0, 1).
    A = sa*z1; B = sb*(rho*z1 + sqrt(1 - rho**2)*z2).
    Return the population sd (divide by n)."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    c = math.sqrt(1 - rho ** 2)
    xs = []
    for _ in range(n):
        z1 = rng.gauss(0, 1)
        z2 = rng.gauss(0, 1)
        xs.append(sa * z1 - h * sb * (rho * z1 + c * z2))
    m = sum(xs) / n
    return math.sqrt(sum((x - m) ** 2 for x in xs) / n)
widget.how: Check runs 11 hidden tests. The ratio and residual sd must be exact. Each simulated sd must be within 3% of the exact one, and the same seed must give the same answer.

hints.text: The residual sd is $\sigma_A\sqrt{1 - \rho^2}$.
In the simulation, draw `z1` before `z2` each day.
Collect `A - h*B` for each day, then take the mean and the population sd.

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check the ratio's order, $\rho\,\sigma_A/\sigma_B$, and divide by n for the sd.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check that each `...` is replaced.

explain.text: The simulated sd sits near 1.2 at $h = 1$ and near 2 at both $h = 0$ and $h = 2$. Doubling the right hedge brings all the risk back, the other way round. The ratio is a minimum, so missing it either side costs.

screens.title: A bank and its sector
screens.prose: A market maker in one bank's shares is long £50,000 after a client sold. The bank moves 2.5% a day. A future on the banking sector moves 1.4% a day, with correlation 0.7.
screens.question: How much of the sector future should they sell, in pounds?

hints.text: Find $h$ first, then scale by the £50,000.

byKey.one: You hedged pound for pound. The bank moves more than the sector, so you need more future.
byKey.rho: You used the correlation alone. Scale it by $2.5/1.4$.
byKey.inv: You put the future's sd on top. The bank is what you hedge.

explain.text: $h = 1.25$, so they sell £62,500 of the future. The risk left is $2.5\% \times \sqrt{1 - 0.49} = 1.79\%$ a day, the bank's own news. A desk that is short calls does the same with shares: it buys the calls' delta.

ideas: Hedge each £1 of A by selling £$h$ of a correlated B, with $h = \rho\,\sigma_A/\sigma_B$.
The best hedge leaves $\sigma_A\sqrt{1 - \rho^2}$: at $\rho = 0.8$, 60% of the sd remains.
Judge a hedge by the risk it removes, not by whether it made money on one roll.

formula.name: Minimum-variance hedge
formula.note: With sds in per cent, $h$ is pounds of B sold for each pound of A held. With sds in pounds a unit, it is units of B for each unit of A.

summary.trap: Hedging pound for pound. If B moves more than A, a ratio of 1 over-hedges the other way.
